name: Security Leadership
guide:
Security Leadership is the discipline of running security as a function, not performing one security task within it. In our current postings this shows up as Chief Information Security Officer, Director of Security, Head of Security, Cybersecurity Manager, and Security Lead. People in these roles set strategy, own budget and headcount, build or run the security organization, and represent security to executives and the board. The day to day is staffing decisions, vendor and program oversight, incident escalation, and tradeoffs between risk and cost, not hands on configuration work. It sits above the individual security disciplines, deciding what gets built and who builds it.

This is different from Security Governance, Risk, and Compliance, which readers often confuse with it. GRC work is the specific job of writing policy, running audits, tracking frameworks like ISO 27001 or SOC 2, and managing regulatory obligations such as GDPR. A GRC analyst or manager can report into a security leader, but that leader's job covers the whole security organization, not just the compliance slice of it. In our data, titles that read as pure GRC work are categorized separately from the Director, Head of Security, and CISO titles that make up this discipline. If a posting is mostly about audits and policy documents, it belongs in Governance, Risk, and Compliance, not here.

On certifications, our tracked skills data for this batch of postings does not tag specific credentials like CISSP or CISM by name, which is worth stating plainly rather than assuming they are required everywhere. What we do see is one federal adjacent posting asking for CSSO and CPSO designations, special programs security officer credentials used in cleared government work, and a general clearance requirement flagged as Security Clearance on another listing. For public sector and defense adjacent roles, a security clearance functions as a hard credential the way CISSP or CISM would elsewhere. Outside government work, our sample leans more on demonstrated program ownership and specific framework experience than on certification badges. Treat named certifications as valuable but not guaranteed by every posting until you read the individual listing.

This is a senior track discipline, and the postings reflect that. Most titles are Manager or Director level, with a smaller group of Lead titles and a distinct set of Executive level Chief Information Security Officer postings at the top. The typical path runs from hands on security engineering or analyst work, through a team lead or manager role owning a specific area like vulnerability management or incident response, and then into a director or CISO role owning the whole function. Federal and defense postings in our sample often require both the operational background and a clearance, which lengthens the path further. Getting to a CISO or Director title generally means years running a security team first, not years doing individual contributor security work alone.

On skills, the postings we track most often name cloud platforms including AWS, GCP, and Azure, along with incident response, vulnerability management, identity and access management, and cloud security broadly. Framework and control references that appear repeatedly include NIST, ISO 27001, SOC 2, Zero Trust, FedRAMP for government adjacent work, and GDPR for postings with a privacy angle. AI governance also shows up as a named skill in a handful of postings, reflecting security leaders increasingly owning oversight of how their organizations use large language models. Beyond technical frameworks, these are leadership roles, so postings also emphasize running a team, working directly with executives, and owning a budget rather than only technical depth. A leader who can speak both languages, the technical framework and the business case, is what these listings are describing.

As of today we currently track approximately 15 open postings in Security Leadership that were newly seen on our most recent scan, out of 98 total postings gathered for this discipline. The single most frequent employer in our sample is Accenture, which accounts for 34 of the 98 postings, nearly all the same Cybersecurity Manager, Utilities Industry role posted separately across dozens of United States cities as part of one hiring campaign rather than 34 distinct openings. Outside that campaign, Nebius appears 5 times across different regional security manager and lead titles, and Maximus appears 4 times across cybersecurity manager postings in different cities. OpenAI, the U.S. Marine Corps, and Staffbase each appear 3 to 4 times in our sample as well. Readers should treat the Accenture count as one large employer's multi city posting rather than 34 separate hiring signals.

On pay, 68 of the 98 postings in our sample include a stated salary figure, while the remaining 30 list none. Among those 68, figures range from about $67,300 a year, an Ensemble Health Partners cybersecurity manager posting, up to $315,000 a year, a Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Chief Information Security Officer posting. That wide spread reflects the mix of manager level and CISO level roles inside one category, plus the many Accenture postings that quote a single point figure rather than a true minimum to maximum range. Federal listings, by contrast, consistently publish real government pay band ranges. Given how much the Accenture campaign and the federal listings pull the numbers apart, we report the observed range rather than a single average.

reading.body:
Security leadership roles across AI companies, infrastructure operators, and adjacent sectors show sustained hiring activity with salaries ranging from $88,089 to $175,542 annually, suggesting security functions remain embedded within broader organizational structures rather than concentrated in pure AI firms.

The distribution of postings reveals two distinct hiring patterns. Specialized AI companies like OpenAI, Cohere, and Nebius are hiring security roles focused on travel, site operations, and reliability engineering, reflecting the physical footprint and supply chain complexity required by infrastructure-heavy AI operations. Meanwhile, traditional enterprise and government contractors are posting security leadership roles at comparable or higher compensation, indicating that demand for these positions extends far beyond the AI sector itself.

The geographic spread and role diversity underscore that security at scale is inseparable from the buildings, supply chains, and geographic distribution that power AI compute. Site security managers, transportation security roles, and regional supply chain positions appear alongside traditional cybersecurity titles. The data does not reveal hiring velocity, whether these represent net growth or replacement cycles, or how security headcount correlates to compute capacity or data center expansion. It shows only that organizations operating large physical and digital infrastructure are actively recruiting security leadership.
